Taylor Ave. in Little Italy, Tuesday, June 30, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That danger is real for vulnerable populations this week, as expected overnight temperatures remain in the upper 70s and low 80s, providing little recovery time after days with heat indexes exceeding 100 degrees.</p><p>"The stress and strain, the dehydration and the poor sleep can build up over several days and lead to worsened outcomes, especially in vulnerable populations," Rao said. “Medically, people need a place to cool down 24 hours a day during this level of extreme heat."</p><p>Sims' organization participated in a 2023 urban heat mapping initiative that found temperatures swung between some parts of the city. On one summer day, Rogers Park on the North Side was 20 degrees cooler than Archer Heights on the Southwest Side, for instance.</p><p>Poorer neighborhoods tend to have less trees and shade, leading to more intense overnight temperatures and limited relief for residents without reliable air conditioning. Those neighborhood also tend to have large areas of concrete and asphalt that absorb and retain heat long after sunset. Some of these communities are farther from Lake Michigan.</p><p>Northwestern University researchers have studied tens of thousands of data points over the last three years to determine who is most likely to get sick or die from extremely hot weather.</p><p>Last year, they presented the findings to City Hall, along with 30 recommendations, including more cooling centers, though it’s not clear how many ideas are being embraced by the city. An updated presentation to the city is expected in the coming weeks.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/28/24017673/southwest-chicago-is-hottest-part-of-city-during-summer-climate-study" target="_blank" >Southwest Side is hottest part of Chicago during summer, climate study finds</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Northwestern also presented the city with a survey of about 500 residents who suggested battling heat waves with more green spaces, water stations at bus and train stops and a number of other ideas. City officials said at the time they would review the suggestions.</p><p></p><p></p><p>The city's response has changed little over past administrations despite decades of research showing the dangers of prolonged heat exposure, said former Chicago Department of Public Health Assistant Commissioner Dr. Howard Ehrman.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" said. "These places are not prepared to accept people en masse anyway."</p><p>Dillon said Chicago's emergency plan should adopt overnight and weekend options. She pointed to Cook County's 24-hour courthouse warming and cooling centers, including the Skokie courthouse, as an example of a more accessible model. entries.title: Union workers rally at manufacturer Woodward MPC's Niles facility
entries.summary: <p>Workers with aerospace manufacturer Woodward MPC joined a practice picket outside its Niles facility on Tuesday, as they urged the company to negotiate a new labor contract.</p><p>The rally came after 71% of UAW Local 5101 members voted last week to authorize a strike. The union said Woodward has stalled contract negotiations for months and committed dozens of unfair labor practices, including disciplining workers and surveillance.</p><p>Nearly 100 workers in red UAW Local 5101 T-shirts rallied in 90 degree heat holding signs that read, “Just practicing for a just contract.”</p><p>Local 5101 has about 850 members, who are production workers at Woodward’s Niles location. The factory makes commercial and military aviation equipment for clients that include Boeing and the U.S. government.</p><p>Workers are fighting for better wages, fair progression, time off and job security. Union leaders said Woodward workers are underpaid compared to industry peers.</p><p>At Tuesday’s rally, Local 5101 President Jose Tapia said, “We make some of the most profitable products in the world on massive contracts for the U.S. government, Boeing and others. We generate millions in profits for our CEO and billions in Wall Street payouts. But we have workers at Woodward who can’t afford to live. They sleep in their cars. They commute two hours a day to work. They haven’t had a raise in years.”</p><p>Tapia, a mechanical assembler with Woodward for 20 years, said the union’s last negotiating session with the company was in October. Woodward offered raises of less than 1%.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f80000" of Local 5101. He said workers at the Niles facility are paid about $16 to $27 an hour, although the aerospace industry’s average wage is closer to $28 to $43 an hour.</p><p>Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss was among elected officials at the rally. Woodward workers “deserve the right to negotiate in good faith and for a fair contract,” Biss said. “Corporations are trying to silence workers. It’s moving and powerful when workers organize and fight back.”</p><p>In September, Woodward workers voted to affiliate with the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America.</p><p>The workers were previously part of an independent union called WMPC Employees Representative Union, founded in 1967. At that time, MPC Products was a smaller, family-owned company. In 2008, it was bought by Woodward, a publicly-listed company based in Colorado.</p><p>Woodward has not recognized the new union. </p><p>A Woodward spokesperson said in a statement: “A case is pending before the National Labor Relations Board regarding union representation for our Niles workforce. We are requesting a government-run election to ensure that every employee’s voice is heard. Until this matter is resolved, negotiations will remain paused. At this time, no strike has been called. Niles operations will continue as usual, and we remain focused on delivering critical controls to our aerospace customers without interruption.”</p><p>In the second quarter, Woodward reported $1.1 billion in sales and $134 million in earnings.</p><p>“A few years ago, I was inspired by the major victories I saw the UAW having at the Big Three and at aerospace employers across the country and decided to try to make my union better,” Tapia said. “All we’re asking is for Woodward to stop breaking the law, and return to the bargaining table. We’ve been forced to file dozens of federal labor charges, for everything from illegal surveillance to unfair discipline to refusing to bargain in good faith. We are just asking to be treated like aerospace workers at employers across the country. We want fair wages for our industry, we want to be able to get a raise, we want to be able to afford to live a decent life with our families."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Defensores de inmigrantes y familias de Chicago sienten alivio tras decisión de Corte Suprema que mantiene la ciudadanía por nacimiento
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON, D.C. — Muchos defensores de Chicago y familias inmigrantes dicen que están “emocionados” y “aliviados” de que la Corte Suprema haya respaldado una amplia definición de <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/birthright-citizenship-immigration-trump-20919d26029cf0f98ecb0dc7f90a066b" target="_blank" >ciudadanía por nacimiento</a>, rechazando la orden ejecutiva del presidente Donald Trump que declaraba que los niños nacidos de personas que están en Estados Unidos ilegal o temporalmente no son ciudadanos estadounidenses.</p><p>“Esto es especialmente personal para mí”, dijo Carson Wang, residente de Chicago e hijo de inmigrantes chinos. Wang mencionó que la ciudadanía por nacimiento le brindó oportunidades que sus amigos sin estatus legal no tuvieron, como asistir a la universidad en la Universidad de Illinois. n“Recibí una beca para ir”, dijo.</p><p>En <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/read-the-supreme-courts-opinion-on-birthright-citizenship-0000019f190fd9d2a19f5b9f9f2e0000" target="_blank" >la decisión de 6-3</a>, los jueces se basaron en una comprensión bien establecida de <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/800b0a2005254ec58369b9564f53be8f" target="_blank" >la 14ª Enmienda</a>, adoptada después de la Guerra Civil, y en leyes federales más recientes para dictaminar que cualquier persona nacida en el país, con excepciones muy limitadas, es ciudadana.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a00000" name="module-a00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las restricciones del presidente republicano estaban detalladas en una orden ejecutiva que firmó el año pasado en el primer día de su segundo mandato. Había sido bloqueada por varias cortes inferiores y no había entrado en vigor en ningún lugar de Estados Unidos.</p><p>“Estoy contenta de que se mantenga”, dijo Gloria, quien dio a luz a un niño en Chicago hace tres semanas. El Chicago Sun-Times no está usando su apellido porque está solicitando asilo y teme ser deportada.</p><p>Había estado preocupada por lo que decidiría la Corte.</p><p>“Ahora me siento más tranquila”, dijo. “Porque la gente seguía diciendo, ‘No, es imposible, ni te preocupes por eso.’ Pero con este presidente, no se sabe”.</p><p>Aún así, no todas sus preocupaciones han desaparecido, comentó. Todavía le preocupa la aplicación de la ley de inmigración. Su esposo es la única fuente de ingresos de la familia y teme que se lo lleven.</p><p>“No miran si tienes antecedentes o no”, dijo. “Solo agarran a las personas”.</p><p>La <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/18/la-ciudadania-por-nacimiento-esta-ante-la-corte-suprema-lo-que-las-familias-de-illinois-deben-saber" target="_blank" >orden de ciudadanía por nacimiento de Trump</a> formaba parte de la campaña de deportación de su administración y de amplias restricciones a la inmigración.</p><p>La orden habría cambiado las ideas ampliamente sostenidas de que <a class="Link" href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-14/" target="_blank" >la 14ª Enmienda</a> otorga ciudadanía a todos los nacidos en Estados Unidos, excluyendo solo a los hijos de diplomáticos extranjeros y a aquellos nacidos de una fuerza ocupante extranjera.</p><p>La enmienda estaba destinada a garantizar que las personas negras, incluyendo los esclavos, tuvieran ciudadanía, aunque la cláusula de ciudadanía está redactada de manera más amplia.</p><p>“Todas las personas nacidas o naturalizadas en los Estados Unidos, y sujetas a la jurisdicción de los mismos, son ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos y del Estado en el que residen”, establece.</p><p>Más de un cuarto de millón de bebés nacidos en los Estados Unidos cada año se habrían visto afectados por la orden ejecutiva, según investigaciones del Instituto de Política Migratoria y del Instituto de Investigación de Población de la Universidad Estatal de Pennsylvania.</p><p>Y algunos defensores en Chicago dicen que aún se preocupan lo que sigue para las comunidades inmigrantes.</p><p>“Aunque estamos aliviados de que la Corte [Suprema] haya respaldado la ciudadanía por nacimiento, no podemos pasar por alto todas las otras decisiones escritas por jueces alineados con MAGA que han socavado nuestros derechos y libertades”, dijo Brandon Lee, portavoz de la Coalición para Derechos de Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois (ICIRR).</p><p>Danae Kovac, directora ejecutiva del HANA Center, una organización por la justicia de inmigrantes, expresó que la decisión de la Corte Suprema generó “sentimientos encontrados”.</p><p>Kovac añadió que la decisión llega en medio de otras resoluciones de la Corte Suprema que han significado “ataques continuos a los inmigrantes”, incluida la eliminación del estatus de protección temporal (TPS) para haitianos y sirios.</p><p>“Es una victoria en un mar de continuos ataques", afirmó Kovac. “Este desafío ha mostrado que la administración actual realmente cree que no hay límites a lo que... perseguirán contra los inmigrantes y contra cualquiera que consideren diferente”.</p><p>Ed Yohnka, portavoz de la ACLU de Illinois, manifestó que mantener la orden ejecutiva habría resultado en “caos” porque nadie sabía cómo se implementaría o aplicaría el cambio.</p><p>La ACLU fue uno de los grupos que impugnaron la orden en las cortes. Yohnka también presentó el caso como parte de una lucha más amplia por la democracia en Estados Unidos.</p><p>“Este caso ha sido parte de un ataque más amplio de la administración contra una democracia diversa e inclusiva”, agregó.</p><p>Kovac dijo que la decisión de la Corte también reafirmó los derechos de las personas a pesar de lo que ella describió como intentos de la administración de definir quién es considerado estadounidense o “americano”.</p><p>“Debemos continuar levantando nuestras voces y declarar claramente que nosotros también somos estadounidenses y que también pertenecemos aquí”, afirmó. “Que la fuerza de [Estados Unidos de] América proviene de su diversidad, proviene de nuestra solidaridad entre nosotros”.</p><p>En un comunicado, el gobernador JB Pritzker calificó la decisión como una “victoria importante” pero dijo que Illinois permanecerá activo y “vigilante en la defensa de la Constitución, defendiendo los derechos que garantiza a cada persona y sostenido los principios que han definido por mucho tiempo nuestra nación”.</p><p>Si bien Trump se ha centrado en gran medida en los inmigrantes sin estatus legal en su retórica y acciones, las restricciones de ciudadanía por nacimiento también habrían aplicado a personas que están legalmente en Estados Unidos, incluidos estudiantes y solicitantes de tarjetas verdes o estatus de residente permanente.</p><p>Para Gloria, la nueva mamá, la decisión del martes significa que su bebé "no tendrá que sufrir", dijo. “Y también tendrá un futuro mejor”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Add some mojo to your chicken dinner
entries.summary: <p>A zingy mojo marinade should be in your grilling repertoire — one that does double duty as both a marinade and a vibrant finishing sauce. “Mojo” is the Spanish word for “sauce,” and it traces its roots to the Canary Islands before traveling to Cuba, Puerto Rico and throughout the Caribbean, where each region developed its own distinctive iteration of the classic condiment.</p><p>Mojo is built on a combination of garlic and citrus, creating a bright, punchy sauce and marinade that infuses and flavors grilled meats, seafood and vegetables. This version comes together with a quick blitz in a blender or food processor. Simply reserve a portion of the sauce for serving, then use the rest to marinate the chicken, allowing the flavors to soak in before the legs hit the grill.</p><p>Traditional mojos often feature sour orange juice for their unique tang. In this recipe, sweet navel orange and fresh lime strike a balance of sweetness and sharp acidity. A generous handful of cilantro, along with jalapeno and onion, lend herbaceous notes and a kick of heat. The result is a fresh, citrusy marinade and sauce that is as versatile as it is delicious. Serve it with grilled meats and fish, roasted vegetables or dolloped over rice and grains.</p><h3>Grilled Mojo Chicken Legs</h3><p>Active time (including grilling time): 1 hour<br>Total time: 1 hour plus marinating time<br>Yield: Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Sauce:</b><br>5 garlic cloves<br>1 medium jalapeno pepper, seeded, coarsely chopped<br>1/2 small yellow onion, chopped<br>1 1/2 cups packed fresh cilantro leaves and tender stems<br>1/2 cup fresh orange juice<br>1/4 cup fresh lime juice<br>1/4 cup olive oil<br>Zest of one orange<br>Zest of one lime<br>1 teaspoon ground cumin<br>1 teaspoon dried oregano<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>4 whole bone-in chicken legs, each 10 to 12 ounces<br>Fresh cilantro<br>Lime and orange wedges</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine the marinade ingredients in the bowl of a food processor. Process to blend. Set aside 1/2 cup for serving.</p><p>Put the chicken a large resealable plastic bag. Add the remaining marinade and seal the bag. Turn the bag to evenly distribute the marinade, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours or up to 24 hours, turning the bag once or twice.</p><p>When ready to grill, remove the chicken from the marinade and place on a plate. Discard the marinade. Prepare the grill for cooking over medium heat.</p><p>Grill the chicken legs over indirect heat for about 30 minutes, then move them to direct heat and continue to cook until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the chicken (not touching the bone) registers 165 degrees, about 10 to 15 minutes more, depending on the size of the legs. Transfer to a platter and let rest for 10 minutes.</p><p>Garnish with fresh cilantro. Serve with lime and orange wedges and the reserved sauce.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago man linked to alleged plot to attack White House UFC event ordered held in jail
entries.summary: <p>A federal prosecutor warned of a “credible threat” to national security heading into the Fourth of July weekend as she convinced a judge Tuesday to detain a Chicago man accused of playing some role in an alleged plot on the Ultimate Fighting Championship event held at the White House.</p><p>A full picture of the role allegedly played by Alexander Iniguez Mercado, 20, has yet to emerge. Assistant U.S. Attorney Elly Moheb argued that’s by Mercado’s design, after he deleted the messaging application Signal from his phone, leading to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/26/trump-white-house-ufc-attack-chicago" target="_blank" >obstruction of justice charges</a>.</p><p>But Mercado’s defense attorney told a judge that Mercado has spoken with the FBI three times, and that he even tried to re-install Signal in an unsuccessful bid to recover any messages that were destroyed when he deleted the encrypted app.</p><p>He said Mercado is a LARPer, which refers to “live action role play,” and is “not interested in any sort of plot” on the event that took place June 14, on President Donald Trump’s birthday.</p><p>U.S. Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes concluded that the allegations against Mercado were serious enough that he should be held in custody.</p><p>Anticipating Mercado would ask to be released into his mother’s custody, the judge pointed to allegations that Mercado hit his mother in the head five times last fall. The incident led to a now-dismissed battery case, Moheb told the judge.</p><p>The judge called the LARPer argument “very interesting, thought provoking and intriguing.”</p><p>But, he said, it “did not reduce the risk enough for me as the judicial officer on a detention motion so that I could be allowed to find that the government had fallen short of its clear-and-convincing evidence burden.”</p><p>Moheb said there’s data showing Mercado deleted Signal from his phone “within minutes” of a June 13 call from an FBI special agent, but Mercado allegedly claimed he uninstalled the app later, at his mother’s direction.</p><p>“That does suggest a level of dishonesty,” Fuentes said.</p><p>Mercado’s two-hour detention hearing at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse also revealed additional details about the alleged plot on the UFC event. Moheb told the judge that Mercado “recruited other individuals” into a Signal messaging group and would “vet” them to determine if they should be allowed in. He allegedly told someone that “peace ain’t the option.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" asked for targets, Mercado allegedly wrote on March 1, “I do have some people in mind. Look I just need you to be patient until the time is right but we can really make history.”</p><p>Still, defense attorney Johanathan Brooks told the judge, “this is essentially something you could read in a Tom Clancy novel. This is not real.” He said the Signal group was about “survivalism,” and there’s “no indication that Mr. Mercado had joined in on this plan.”</p><p>Mercado told the FBI “everything he knows,” Brooks said.</p><p>Federal prosecutors have charged at least seven others in connection with the alleged plot to attack the UFC event. It involved a plan to deploy drones armed with explosives into the event to force an evacuation, allowing snipers to open fire on “high value targets,” Justice Department officials have claimed.</p><p>Moheb pointed to evidence Tuesday that it might have been a precursor to additional attacks leading up to the Fourth of July. She argued that most people involved in the planning are still at large, with the nation’s 250th anniversary coming up in a matter of days.</p><p>“The government believes that the defendant can contribute to that credible threat,” Moheb said.</p><p>The indictment against Mercado, made public last week, does not actually allege he participated in the planning. Rather, it said the FBI “obtained information” that he was a “member and an administrator” of Signal messaging groups where people “appeared to communicate with others” about the attack.</p><p>Then, on June 13, an FBI special agent called Mercado “to discuss threats made online” about the event and asked Mercado whether he planned to travel to the nation’s capital to help with the attack, according to the indictment.</p><p>Mercado allegedly denied it and said he did not want to meet with the agent.</p><p>“After a brief conversation, the call was disconnected,” the indictment said.</p><p>The FBI agent apparently reached out to Mercado again to set up an interview, according to the indictment. It said Mercado “did not initially respond.”</p><p>Mercado is then accused of uninstalling Signal from his phone between June 13 and June 14, the day of the UFC event. Uninstalling the application deletes the user’s messages, the indictment said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/26/trump-white-house-ufc-attack-chicago" target="_blank" >Chicago man charged in relation to alleged plot to attack White House UFC event</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicken souvlaki skewers with tzatziki sauce an easy, fun dinner made for sharing
entries.summary: <p>This light, herbaceous chicken dinner is refreshingly easy to prepare. A simple marinade of lemon, garlic and spice infuses the chicken with bright flavor, deepened by the smoky char from the grill. When ready to cook, simply the thread the strips of meat onto skewers, which exposes the lengthy edges, allowing them to caramelize and crisp. Grill until lightly charred (or use a stovetop griddle for indoor cooking), then serve them on a platter for fun, build-your-own assembly.</p><p>This dish is undemanding and flexible, equally suited to a weeknight dinner or a casual outdoor meal. The chicken and creamy, garlicky tzatziki sauce can be prepared up to 24 hours in advance. If preparing the tzatziki ahead, wait to add the fresh mint and dill until just before serving to preserve their brightness. Serve alongside warm pita bread and crisp garden vegetables and let everyone assemble their own plates.</p><h3>Chicken Souvlaki Skewers With Tzatziki Sauce</h3><p><b>Yield:</b> Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Marinade:</b><br>1/4 cup olive oil<br>3 garlic cloves, grated<br>2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice<br>1 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest<br>1 teaspoon dried oregano<br>1 teaspoon sweet paprika<br>1 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>2 pounds boneless skinless chicken thighs<br>Kosher salt and black pepper</p><p><b>Tzatziki:</b><br>1 1/2 cups whole-milk Greek yogurt<br>1/2 English cucumber, seeded, finely diced (about 1 cup)<br>2 garlic cloves, grated<br>1 tablespoon olive oil<br>1 tablespoon fresh lemon juice<br>1/4 cup chopped fresh mint leaves<br>2 tablespoons chopped fresh dill sprigs<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper</p><p><b>Assembly:</b><br>Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper<br>Butter lettuce leaves<br>2 vine-ripened tomatoes, sliced<br>1 small red onion, halved and thinly sliced<br>Fresh mint leaves<br>Pita bread, warmed</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine the marinade ingredients in a small bowl and whisk to blend.</p><p>Halve each chicken thigh lengthwise. Place the chicken in a large bowl. Pour in the marinade and stir to thoroughly coat the meat. Cover the bowl and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes or up to 24 hours.</p><p>Combine the tzatziki ingredients in a bowl and stir to blend. Cover and refrigerate until use. (The tzatziki can be prepared up to 24 hours in advance. If preparing in advance, omit the fresh mint and dill, stirring them in just before serving.)</p><p>Remove the chicken pieces from the marinade and thread on skewers. Discard any remaining marinade.</p><p>Grill the skewers over direct medium-high heat until they are charred in spots and cooked through, 8 to 10 minutes.</p><p>Slide the chicken off the skewers onto a serving platter. Lightly season with additional salt and black pepper. Serve the chicken with lettuce, tomatoes, onion, mint leaves, pita bread and the tzatziki sauce.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>

entries.title: Pritzker issues disaster proclamation for recent storms, tornadoes and flooding
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker issued a disaster proclamation following severe weather, flooding and tornadoes over the last several months.</p><p>The move frees up state resources, including funds and personnel, while expediting the contract and procurement process for local governments to help speed up recovery, Pritzker said in a statement Tuesday.</p><p>The proclamation covers months of storms, from the tornadoes that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/03/12/kankakee-county-tornado-damage-amount-state-relief-funds" target="_blank" ><u>tore through Kankakee in March</u></a> to the most recent storms June 21 in Jefferson County, including: April 14 and 17 in Stephenson County; April 17 in Winnebago County; April 17 and 18 in McLean County; <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/11/obstruction-on-tracks-causes-service-disruption-on-cta-yellow-line-trains-after-storms" target="_blank" ><u>June 10 in Cook County</u></a>; <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/11/tornado-watch-chicago-area-weather-severe-storms" target="_blank" ><u>June 11 in LaSalle and Woodford Counties</u></a>; and June 17 in Coles, Effingham and Warren Counties.</p><p>The state is also working to identify if any federal funds are available to assist as well, Pritzker’s office said. Smaller, rural communities can qualify for the Community Development Block Grant <a class="Link" href="https://prezlymail.com/c/622eb4c1-4215-4b4e-a7df-0b37a91d0426/0e18f1a2/https%3A%2F%2Fdceo.illinois.gov%2Fcommunitydevelopment%2Fpublicinfrastructuresetaside.html" target="_blank" ><u>Disaster Response</u></a> program, which is funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and offers up to $250,000 for local governments impacted by the disaster, Pritzker’s office said.</p><p>“Illinois has faced unprecedented severe weather this year, and I remain committed to supporting every community, business, and family as they rebuild," Pritzker said in the statement. "As communities recover, we remember the lives that were lost and hold their families and loved ones in our thoughts during this difficult time.”</p>

entries.title: How to grill vegetables and toss them in Isaac Toups’ bacon vinaigrette
entries.summary: <p>Want to make your vegetables taste better and have your friends love you? Char the hell out of some on the grill and then toss them in a bacon vinaigrette, using this recipe from my cookbook "Chasing the Gator: Isaac Toups and the New Cajun Cooking."</p><p>These are vegetables so unhealthy a Cajun might actually eat them.</p><p>You can do this dish year-round with whatever is in season: eggplant and zucchini, radishes, green beans, radicchio or others. If the vegetable is sliceable, slice it. If it's broccoli or cauliflower, cut into quarter-size florets; if green beans, leave them whole.</p><h3>Grilled Garden Vegetables with Bacon Vinaigrette</h3><p>From the cookbook "Chasing the Gator," by Isaac Toups and Jennifer V. Cole</p><p><b>Yield:</b> 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>8 slices thick-cut bacon<br>5 cloves garlic, peeled<br>3 anchovy filets<br>½ cup apple cider vinegar<br>½ cup canola oil<br>1 pound assorted vegetables, cut into ¼-inch slices<br>1 ½ teaspoons kosher salt<br>1 teaspoon ground black pepper<br>½ teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes<br>1 tablespoon extra virgin olive oil</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Preheat the grill to high (about 500°F). Preheat the oven to 400°F.</p><p>Place the bacon slices on a rimmed baking sheet and cook in the oven for about 20 minutes, until the bacon is crispy. Remove the bacon and reserve the baking sheet with the rendered fat. Crumble the bacon and set aside.</p><p>In a blender, combine the garlic, anchovies, and vinegar and put the lid on. Turn the blender on and slowly drizzle in the canola oil. This is never going to be a fully emulsified vinaigrette, so don't fret if it looks like it's breaking. Add the reserved bacon fat (about 1½ tablespoons, but if you have more from cooking your bacon, just toss it all in) and keep the blender buzzing for 5 seconds to combine all the ingredients. Keep warm. I like to put it in a metal container, like a mixing bowl, and keep it by the grill while I cook the vegetables. The vinaigrette doesn't need to be hot, just not too cold because the bacon fat will congeal if you let it.</p><p>In a large bowl or on a rimmed baking sheet, toss the vegetables with the salt, pepper, pepper flakes and olive oil. Place the vegetables on the hot grill in a single layer and cook on each side for about 2 minutes. They should char on the outside while keeping the crunch or snap of fresh crudités. They should be really crispy and charred, not all wimpy and overcooked; high heat is key here. Remove the vegetables from the grill and put in a nonreactive bowl.</p><p>Toss the grilled vegetables in the bacon vinaigrette. Top with the crumbled bacon. Serve.</p><p><i>Isaac Toups has four times been named a James Beard Best Chef of the South semi-finalist or finalist since opening Toups' Meatery in New Orleans in 2012 with his wife, Amanda. He was named an Eater Young Gun of the South, Eater New Orleans' Chef of the Year, and appears on Top Chef. He is a passionate advocate for the protection of America's wetlands. Jennifer V. Cole spent nearly a decade at Southern Living magazine, where she served as deputy editor and wrote annual restaurant lists. Her writing appears in food and lifestyle publications.</i></p><p><i>Excerpted from "Chasing the Gator" by Isaac Toups and Jennifer V. Cole. Copyright (copyright) 2018 by Isaac Toups. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company. New York, NY. All rights reserved.</i></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks likely to avoid silly contracts — aside from Bowen Byram — in NHL free agency
entries.summary: <p>The NHL's weakest free-agent market in recent memory, strongest trade market in recent memory and fastest-rising salary cap in history creates a strange dynamic heading into Wednesday.</p><p>That dynamic is particularly strange for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*1cia8zd*_up*MQ..*_ga*MjA4MzQ4OTAyNy4xNzgyODU2NzUw*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODI4NTY3NDkkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI4NTY3NTIkajU3JGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> as general manager Kyle Davidson tries to straddle the line between building for the future and accelerating the timeline.</p><p>The opening of free agency at 11 a.m. CT on July 1 is typically a seismic event in the hockey calendar, and it may still be this year — but not for the usual reason.</p><p>Plenty of free agents will still sign with new teams, but few are major-impact players. It's telling that the highest-scoring UFAs available are Anthony Mantha, who's far from a household name, and Alex Ovechkin, a household name who's 40 years old.</p><p>The highest-scoring free agent under the age of 31 is Matias Maccelli, who tallied all of 39 points last season. And among all UFA defensemen, only four recorded more than 27 points last season.</p><p>Yet plenty will still get paid large sums Wednesday (and beyond) because most teams have boatloads of cap space to play with — and because such a strong anti-rebuilding culture has overtaken the league's GMs.</p><p>Every GM wants to improve his team and has ample means, yet scarce opportunities, to do so. The resulting mindset of desperation is going to lead to some dumb, regrettable contracts getting handed out.</p><p>One of those, in fact, may go to new Hawks defenseman Bowen Byram, whom Davidson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/06/24/blackhawks-bowen-byram-elite-defenseman-chicago-trade-kyle-davidson?_gl=1*vqv1dm*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTE0OTg4MjY2OS4xNzgyODU3Nzk2*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODI4NTc3OTYkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI4NTc3OTYkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >acquired last week</a> knowing full well he would have to "put our money where our mouth is" to re-sign him. </p><p>Since Byram currently sits just one year away from UFA status and knows the Hawks just gave the Sabres three valuable assets to acquire him, he holds almost all leverage.</p><p>Byram said he intended to sign in Chicago long-term, and it sounds like he indeed will. But he's about to at least temporarily become one of the league's highest-paid defensemen — his cap hit will almost certainly exceed $10 million — even though he hasn't yet proven he's a No. 1.</p><p>The Byram extension is one basically guaranteed piece of Hawks news Wednesday. Will there be much other news? That remains to be seen.</p><p>The Hawks could dabble in the free-agent market, perhaps to add a veteran defenseman. John Carlson and Jacob Trouba are the two most prominent names in that category. Penalty-killing forward Ilya Mikheyev could also circle back to them if unimpressed by his offers.</p><p>But since Davidson isn't seeking depth — he has more than enough youngsters and prospects ready to compete for roster spots — he likely won't be too active quantity-wise.</p><p>Odds are Davidson won't be too active on the trade market, either, but if he does do something on that front, it's more likely to be significant.</p><p>Stars winger Jason Robertson, a restricted free agent, remains available, the drama around his situation having taken a brief pause after many twists and turns last week. </p><p>But would the Stars be willing to trade him for solely picks and prospects? Would Robertson be willing to sign with the Hawks? And would Davidson be willing to pay him $15 million or more?</p><p>The Hawks aren't in the conversation for the three American stars — Dylan Larkin, Zach Werenski and Connor Hellebuyck — trying to force their way out of struggling teams, but when and where they each move will send domino effects throughout the market.</p><p>There are a decent number of other top-six forwards available — including Matthew Knies (Maple Leafs), Kirill Marchenko (Blue Jackets), Jake DeBrusk (Canucks), Rickard Rakell (Penguins) and Tomas Hertl (Golden Knights) — but they're all either aging or would cost a ton to acquire.</p><p>Meanwhile, a new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/06/29/blackhawks-qualifying-offers-nhl-free-agents-connor-bedard-kevin-korchinski?_gl=1*qmob46*_up*MQ..*_ga*MjA4MzQ4OTAyNy4xNzgyODU2NzUw*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODI4NTY3NDkkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI4NTY3NDkkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Connor Bedard contract</a> doesn't seem imminent, even though that is one other piece of big Hawks news that will arrive at some point this summer.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore entries.title: Chicagoans step up to aid earthquake victims in Venezuela
entries.summary: <p>On a warm, muggy Monday night Dani Salazar lifted boxes and bags from cars and SUVs and carried them into the basement of the Coppin Community Center in the Washington Park neighborhood.</p><p>Vehicles pulled up by the dozens to drop off needed supplies to the free store La Tiendita. Their ultimate destination: Venezuela, where hundreds died and many more are still missing from two earthquakes that hit less than a week ago.</p><p>"I have a cousin who lived in a high rise in Caracas that completely collapsed,” 26-year-old Salazar said. “Thankfully no one in my extended family has died or been seriously hurt. I know that’s not the case for everybody.”</p><p>Salazar moved to the United States when he was 11 years old. He arrived in Chicago three years ago but still keeps in touch with family in Venezuela.</p><p>“I’ve been able to stay in communication with them through WhatsApp,” he said. “I’ve been volunteering here for a couple of years.”</p><p>La Tiendita ("Little Shop"), 5627 S. Michigan Ave, opened in 2022 as a food pantry and free store when Venezuelan migrants were sent to Chicago by the busloads from Texas.</p><p>Now it’s been turned into a drop-off point for those wanting to donate to victims of the earthquake.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" The store is currently collecting donations for those affected by the recent earthquakes in Venezuela.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Arcelia Guerrero is president of MESA Chicago (Mutual Aid for Immigrants), a grassroots community organization that supports recently arrived immigrant families with essential resources, groceries, and helps to run La Tiendita.”</p><p>“I’m getting a lot of text messages and email messages. I have people come and drop off items. We just spread the word a few days ago, last Thursday, so slowly, but it's coming," Guerrero said.</p><p>Guerrero, who is Mexican-American, said her group is looking for items such as medications, diapers, baby wipes, toothpaste, toothbrushes, deodorants, and personal hygiene items, alcohol, gauze, bandages.</p><p>There’s even a need for the rescue volunteers on the ground such as gloves, face masks, safety goggles, and personal protective equipment.</p><p>“We have about 30 to 40 boxes of items. We’re hoping to fill a U-Haul and then drive it to Miami,” Guerrero said.</p><p>Other groups are also getting set to deliver donated items to Miami.</p><p>On Tuesday afternoon, volunteers with the Illinois Venezuelan Alliance were loading some 250 boxes onto a large truck in Little Village that will eventually make its way to Miami later this week.</p><p>From there, the disaster relief data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A volunteer holds up a Venezuelan flag in the La Tiendita free store housed in the basement of the Coppin Community Center in Washington Park on the South Side, Monday, June 29, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Venezuelans know that Venezuela has been in a crisis for a long time, and this is just a catastrophe that fell upon the Venezuelan people,” said Luciano Pedota, interim executive director of the Little Village-based alliance. “Inflation has been very high. The economy in Venezuela has been in shackles. The political situation, the health system has really deteriorated. The situation in Venezuela is bad. The need is huge.”</p><p>Pedota said for those wanting to help, the best way is to donate money.</p><p>“We can collect a lot of goods here, but we still need to pay for transportation. We need to send transportation or boxes to Miami or directly to Venezuela, and so that costs money,” Pedota said.</p><p>Pedota said the alliance will continue to collect donated items as long as there is a need.</p><p>“We decided that we were going to continue to receive as long as people wanted to donate goods, until it slows down. We anticipate this is going to be an ongoing crisis for, for several months ... and who knows, maybe even a year,” he said.</p><p>Like many natives of Venezuela, the 59-year-old Pedota said he had relatives, including his mother, who were affected by the quakes but not injured.</p><p>“I have relatives who thank God were in zones that were not affected nearly as much, but they still. I mean, yesterday my mom felt that there was a second kind of shake,” he said.</p><p>Pedota said he is thankful other Chicagoans, and especially other Latino groups were donating items.</p><p>“Everybody is stepping up. A lot of people are aware of the situation in Venezuela, and they know that this is compounding, exacerbating something that was already a dire situation,” Pedota said. “A lot of people are calling me, asking me how they can help. I sent them to our <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilvenalliance.org/" target="_blank" >website</a>.”</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and weekend anchor for WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Video footage shows fatal Oak Park police shooting at gas station
entries.summary: <p>Video footage released Tuesday shows an Oak Park police officer firing nine shots as a man he had pulled over at a gas station ran away, fatally shooting him.</p><p>The officer had stopped Christian Wallace, 38, just after 9 p.m. May 31 at a gas station at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/01/oak-park-police-say-officer-fatally-shot-man-after-fight-during-traffic-stop" target="_blank" >Harrison Street and Austin Boulevard</a>, Oak Park police have said.</p><p>In body-worn camera footage, the officer tells Wallace that he failed to use a turn signal when changing lanes, and he signaled too late when turning into the gas station.</p><p>Wallace provides his driver’s license and insurance at the officer’s request. The officer later says he smells alcohol in the car and Wallace shows him a red solo cup filled with a small amount of alcohol, which the officer says he’s “not worried about.”</p><p>The officer tells Wallace to exit the car, at which point Wallace gets out and steps aside to be searched. At one point, the officer appears to feel something on Wallace and asks, “What’s that?”</p><p>The body-camera footage is not visible at this point, but video from the officer’s squad car shows a struggle ensuing over a gun found on Wallace.</p><p>“Do not reach, bro, you’re gonna get Tased. Do not reach or you’re gonna get shot,” the officer yells. “... Do not reach for that f------ gun or you’re gonna get shot. Do you hear me? It’s not worth it.”</p><p>The officer continuously asks on his radio for backup and says, “He has a gun.”</p><p>Wallace and the officer wrestle on the ground for a moment until Wallace breaks free.</p><p>That’s when the officer opens fire and Wallace runs away through the gas station parking lot as the officer continues shooting.</p><p>“Shots fired! Shots fired!” the officer yells through his radio.</p><p>Body-worn cameras from two other responding officers show the initial officer and other officers rendering aid to Wallace.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/rLc4l5-0Dpc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Oak Park Police Department - Footage released from officer-involved shooting (May 31, 2026)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Wallace suffered four gunshot wounds and was pronounced dead that night at Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, police said.</p><p>The officer who fired shots was taken to the same hospital and released the next day. He remains on medical leave from an injury he suffered during the incident, Oak Park officials said.</p><p>“My heart continues to be with the family and friends of Christian Wallace during this incredibly difficult time,” Oak Park village President Vicki Scaman said in a statement. “Until now, the video was withheld so that the Public Integrity Task Force could maintain the integrity of its investigation. Today, we can take an important step toward transparency owed to those family and friends, and to the entire community, with the release of the footage.”</p><p>Oak Park Police Chief Shatonya Johnson said the shooting remains under investigation by the Illinois State Police.</p><p>“The Oak Park Police Department remains committed to transparency, accountability and treating every person with dignity and respect, with the preservation of human life at the center of everything we do,” Johnson said. “We will continue to provide information as appropriate while honoring the integrity of the investigation."</p>

entries.title: Judge dismisses Edgewater residents, businesses' lawsuit over Broadway zoning changes
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County circuit judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit arguing that two city ordinances upzoning nearly 2 miles of Broadway, from Montrose to Devon avenues, should be overturned.</p><p>The Broadway land use plan, approved in October 2025, includes more than 20 ordinances impacting what could be built along the central commercial corridor. The new zoning classification allows for buildings up to 80 feet and “a series of uses that are incompatible with the existing neighborhood,” according to the Edgewater Residents for Responsible Development's complaint, such as gas stations, hotels, large entertainment venues, recycling facilities and crematoriums.</p><p>The Edgewater Residents group, along with 13 businesses and residents, sued the city of Chicago in January, with the city filing a motion to dismiss in March.</p><p>“As an organization dedicated to Chicagoans’ right to participate in government decisions that directly affect their neighborhoods and their lives, we are shocked by this decision,” Patricia Sharkey, president of ERRD, said in a news release. “ERRD and its co-plaintiffs will be evaluating their next steps, but this is too important to the lives of Edgewater residents and businesses for this narrow view of citizens’ rights to be the last word. An appeal is likely.”</p><p>Judge Neil Cohen said in his decision that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate how residents were deprived of their constitutionally protected interests, or how nearby residents were prejudiced by the city’s rollout of its public hearings and public comment period. </p><p>Last year, the Broadway development framework plan was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/02/20/chicago-plan-commmission-framework-upzoning-broadway-devon-montrose" >endorsed 12-1</a> by the Chicago Plan Commission, after two hours of public testimony where most speakers were in opposition to the zoning changes. The commission also received about 450 pages of written comments before its meeting, with the majority supporting the proposal.</p><p>It took months for the proposal to reach the Committee on Zoning, Landmarks and Building Standards — largely because of an issue pointed out in the lawsuit. The plaintiffs said they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/10/14/neighbors-uproar-chicago-zoning-committee-broadway-zoning-uptown-development" >weren’t given advance written notices</a> about hearings for Broadway’s upzoning and that a “lottery system” for public speakers at the city’s zoning committee meeting denied them the chance to testify about the changes.</p><p>Ald. Bennett Lawson (44th), then-temporary zoning chairman, said during the committee meeting that the city met its obligations to notify property owners. He said many notices posted along the street were torn down or defaced, but they were replaced.</p><p>The city argued in its motion to dismiss the case that even if procedural due process violations occurred, Edgewater residents failed to show the impact of those violations in their lawsuit.</p><p>Cohen agreed and said a zoning classification is not a protected interest — either for a property owner or an adjacent property owner.</p><p>“The ordinances have not deprived the property-owning Plaintiffs of any of their current uses of their properties, but rather have increased the permissible uses of their properties,” Cohen wrote in his decision.</p><p>The ERRD had asked the court to revert the zoning to its previous classifications, invalidating the ordinances. The group has said it isn’t against new development in Edgewater, but rather the lack of public input and collaboration on crafting the plan.</p><p>Separately, the group issued a call in early June for the Chicago Park District to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/04/edgewater-residents-emanuel-congregation-land-public-park" target="_blank" >purchase an Edgewater synagogue’</a>s lakefront property in order to block their development proposal and preserve the land as open park and beach space.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/13/edgewater-residents-businesses-sue-chicago-broadway-zoning-changes" >Edgewater residents, businesses sue city over Broadway zoning changes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicago’s top cop names new No. 2, promoting detectives’ chief Antoinette Ursitti
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police Supt. Larry Snelling named a new second-in-command on Tuesday, over eight months after the top cop’s last first deputy superintendent resigned.</p><p>Antoinette Ursitti, a 25-year veteran of the department, was tapped for the role after serving three years as the department’s chief of detectives, according to a statement from the police department.</p><p>Kevin Bruno, the deputy chief of the detectives bureau, will replace Ursitti, the department said. Snelling also promoted Cmdr. Ricky Rivera to deputy chief of Area Five and made six other police supervisors commanders.</p><p>“Throughout their careers, our newly promoted leaders have worked on behalf of their fellow Chicagoans to strengthen safety across our communities for every resident and family," Snelling wrote. "Their knowledge and experience in implementing effective strategies to combat and prevent crime are why they were selected for their new assignments."</p><p>Yolanda Talley, Ursitti’s predecessor, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/22/chicago-police-yolanda-talley-larry-snelling-retire" target="_blank" ><u>resigned as first deputy superintendent last fall</u></a> after just seven months on the job. </p><p>Talley stepped into the role in March 2025 after Snelling left the post vacant for the first 17 months of his tenure. She was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/03/17/chicago-top-cop-yolanda-talley-heroin-bust-car-niece" target="_blank" ><u>the first Black woman to hold the position.</u></a> </p><p>Talley had previously been embroiled in a bizarre incident that involved a drug bust, her niece and her personal vehicle, though the city’s inspector general’s office ultimately found Talley hadn’t broken any rules. Just months after her promotion, Snelling began significantly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/07/31/chicago-police-department-cpd-larry-snelling-yolanda-talley" target="_blank" >scaling back Talley’s duties</a>.</p><p>The police department described Ursitti as "a purpose-driven leader who prioritizes the well-being of her fellow CPD members and the people of Chicago."</p><p>“She will oversee day-to-day operations across the department and step into her new role with more than two decades of experience across many areas of CPD," the department said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/22/chicago-police-yolanda-talley-larry-snelling-retire" target="_blank" >Yolanda Talley stepping down after just months as CPD’s second-in-command</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/03/17/chicago-top-cop-yolanda-talley-heroin-bust-car-niece" target="_blank" >Chicago’s top cop names Yolanda Talley new second-in-command, first woman to hold post</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/07/31/chicago-police-department-cpd-larry-snelling-yolanda-talley" target="_blank" >Chicago’s top cop consolidates power by scaling back No. 2’s role</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man who posed as drug lord Pablo Escobar's son gets 6 years in prison for 'terrorizing' Chicago business partner
entries.summary: <p>A Moroccan man who claimed he was the son of notorious drug kingpin Pablo Escobar was sentenced Tuesday to six and a half years in federal prison for beating and threatening to kill his Chicago business partner over a $1.5 million debt he insisted he was owed. </p><p>Jawad Fakroune, 46, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/27/extortion-stefani-jawad-fakroune-conviction-fbi-restaurants-chicago" target="_blank" >convicted of extortion</a> in January after prosecutors said he terrorized restaurant owner Adolfo Garcia by assaulting him and threatening to kill him and his family unless he paid up. </p><p>"You are a lawless, violent bully," U.S. District Judge Manish Shah told Fakroune before sentencing him. "Nothing suggests you have any interest in redemption."</p><p>In addition to his 78-month prison term, Fakroune was fined $50,000. After he completes his time behind bars, the federal Department of Homeland Security will evaluate whether Fakroune should be deported.</p><p>Fakroune's sentencing comes as he faces an even broader legal fight. He's separately charged in federal court with cheating investors out of millions of dollars through sham ventures, including a shipping container company and a marijuana farm, while dodging taxes and using the money to bankroll a lavish lifestyle. </p><p>Prosecutors said that money paid for a sprawling Lemont estate, a New York City apartment, luxury cars and high-end watches.</p><p>Fakroune cultivated an image as a wealthy international businessman, at times telling people he was the son of Escobar, the late Colombian drug lord. </p><p>His criminal history stretched back years. In 2008, he was convicted in New York of bribery and theft and served about four years behind bars.</p><p>Even so, Fakroune had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/08/28/fbi-irs-moroccan-fraud-tax-evasion-chicago-police-pritzker" target="_blank" >built relationships with influential figures</a> in Chicago's business and political circles, including former Gov. JB Pritzker aide Lisa Duarte, Tavern on Rush owner Phil Stefani and Illinois Sports Facilities Authority board member Patricia "Trish" Rooney. They weren't accused of any wrongdoing.</p><p>Fakroune became a "Robin Hood of Rush Street" of sorts, buying drinks for people on the upscale strip of bars and restaurants in the Gold Coast, but those same pals have since abandoned him, his lawyer Damon Cheronis said.</p><p>Before he was sentenced, Fakroune told the judge he had lost control of himself when he beat Garcia.</p><p>"I am sorry I hurt him, I am sorry I scared him," said Fakroune, who was wearing an orange jail suit with his long salt-and-pepper hair pulled back in a knot.</p><p>But prosecutors said Fakroune's crime wasn't a spur-of-the-moment act of violence.</p><p>"This was a campaign of terror executed over several years," Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard Rothblatt said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Wacker Drive in January 2014.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Rothblatt read a victim impact statement from Garcia, who had owned several Chicago restaurants including Yours Truly, a River North oyster and martini bar, where the beating happened on Nov. 25, 2025.</p><p>"I felt hopeless, suicidal and completely defeated," Garcia wrote. </p><p>"I am always watching over my shoulder," he added.</p><p>Garcia said his restaurant business is gone and he now works in a construction job.</p><p>In a court filing, Fakroune's lawyer Cheronis suggested that the government had exaggerated Fakroune’s animosity toward Garcia. He pointed to messages the two had exchanged before the FBI launched its investigation in 2024, in which Fakroune and Garcia called each other "brother." </p><p>Cheronis also portrayed Garcia as a dishonest business partner and unreliable government witness.</p><p>"This was not the typical extortion that you see," Cheronis said in court Tuesday. "It was a very messy situation."</p><p>Fakroune said he was born into poverty in 1979 in Casablanca, Morocco, where he witnessed machete fights and was tortured by law enforcement officials before immigrating to the United States in 2001. He lived in Boston and New York before settling in Chicago.</p><p>But the judge said Fakroune's difficult upbringing in Morocco didn't have a bearing on his sentence. He noted his New York convictions, his possession of guns as a felon and his attempts to evade the FBI.</p><p>He called Fakroune a "sophisticated criminal."</p><p>In late 2024, Fakroune slipped away from the FBI during a raid on his New York apartment. He was dressed only in a black garbage bag when he walked into an upscale Italian restaurant, obtaining clothes and disappearing, authorities said. </p><p>His run from federal agents ended in early 2025 when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/20/extortion-chicago-pritzker-fbi-restaurants-phil-stefani-jawad-fakroune" target="_blank" >the FBI tracked him to a hideout</a> in Michigan City, Indiana, where he was living under an alias.
